To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the information provided in visual inertial structure-from-motion with 3 accelerometers, 3 gyroscopes, and a monocular camera is redundant, and that the observability of the system is not affected by removing all the gyroscopes and 3 accelerometers.

1) the observability properties are the same if 3 gyroscopes are removed; 2) the observability is lost if the camera is uncalibrated and one more accelerometer is removed; 3) the observability does not change if the camera is calibrated and one more accelerometer (and one gyroscope) is removed.

the observability of visual inertial SfM does not change by removing 2 gyroscopes, 1 accelerometer and the extrinsic camera calibration, and that this system can be used to understand the vestibular and visual system in the human brain.

the observability properties and the minimum number of sensors required to estimate the 6 degrees of freedom of a rigid body in motion from visual inertial measurements.
the study of the observability properties and minimum number of sensors for the visual-inertial structure-from-motion system.
the study of visual inertial systems, and more precisely the analysis of the minimum number of sensors needed to guarantee the observability of the system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observability of the visual inertual system is not influenced by the removal of all the 3 gyros and 1 accelerometer, while the system loses part (or all) of its observability when 1 accelerometer is further removed, depending on whether the camera is extrinsicly calibrated or not.
visual inertial structure-from-motion is observable with a monocular camera plus 1 accelerometer, and that it is observable with a camera plus 2 accelerometers, if the camera calibration is known.
the information provided in the standard visual-inertial structure-from-motion is redundant and the observability properties are preserved by reducing the number of sensors from 6 to 2 or 3.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paper shows that the information from the inertial sensors can be replaced by the information from the monocular camera.
the paper shows that the information given by a monocular vision and 3 accelerometers is sufficient for estimating the 6 degrees of freedom of a rigid body.

this paper provides the first analysis of the observability properties when the number of inertia sensors is reduced, and introduces an original method in control theory to analyze non linear systems with unknown input control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a monocular camera can provide the same observability property as 3 accelerometers, 3 gyroscopes, and a camera, when the camera is extrinsicly calibrated.
the information provided in the standard formulation of visual inertial SLAM is redundant and the system can be simplified without loss of observability properties.
the visual inertial system can still be observable when only a monocular camera is available, and 1 or even 2 accelerometers are used.
